← Previous05 · Synthetic Data→ Next05.2 · Evol-Instruct, Chain-of-Thought, and Quality Control
05.2Chapter 5 · Synthetic Data

Evol-Instruct, Chain-of-Thought, and Quality Control

Data generate karna aadha kaam hai — use evolve karna, reasoning sikhana aur quality control karna baaki aadha hai. Bina inke aapka dataset uniform difficulty ka, flat answers wala aur hallucinations se bhara hoga — aur student wahi sab high confidence se seekh lega. Is section me teeno techniques hain.

Evol-Instruct — simple questions ko complex banao

Instruction fine-tuning ki key challenge complexity ki wide range cover karna hai. Human-written instructions common, relatively simple tasks ke aas-paas cluster karte hain, aur scale karna mushkil hota hai. Evol-Instruct technique seed instructions ko automatically evolve karke progressively zyada complex aur diverse variants banati hai. Operations me shamil hain: constraints add karna (patient pregnant hai aur use penicillin allergy hai), deeper reasoning (psychological mechanism explain karo), specificity badhana (stage 3 CKD, eGFR 35 par focus karo), aur scope widen karna (existing diabetes management plan ke saath interaction bhi address karo).

Example: "What are the treatment options for GERD?" evolve hokar banta hai "What are the treatment options for GERD in a 72-year-old who is already taking clopidogrel after a stent placement?" — ek sawaal jo age aur drug interactions dono ko consider karta hai. Practical rule of thumb: sirf 20–30% examples evolve karo, har simple example ko ek baar evolve karke harder variant banao. Aur anchoring se savdhaan raho — agar wahi 72-year-old wala example ekmatra template hai, to evolved dataset me suspiciously zyada 72-year-olds aa jayenge!

Critical detail: answer hamesha regenerate karo. Evolved question ko original answer ke saath pair mat karo — naye constraints outcome badal sakte hain, aur original answer evolved question ka jawab hi nahi deta. Teacher ko evolved question ka bilkul fresh answer likhne do, jaise woh brand-new question ho. Answer ko patch karne ki koshish se original text me ek paragraph awkwardly bolt-on ho jaata hai. Loop ye hai: question evolve karo, verify karo ki woh abhi bhi sense banata hai, phir teacher se fresh answer mango. Result ek natural difficulty gradient hota hai — kuch straightforward, kuch moderately complex, kuch real clinical nuance wale.

Chain-of-thought data — reasoning dikhao, sirf conclusion nahi

Model ko apna kaam dikhana ho to training data me reasoning trace honi chahiye, sirf conclusion nahi. CoT examples ke liye system prompt structured reasoning demand karta hai, labelled sections ke saath: CLINICAL CONSIDERATIONS (2–3 sentences me key clinical considerations), REASONING (differential ya decision points step by step), aur RECOMMENDATION (clear rationale ke saath). Aise examples par train hua student conclusion par seedha jump karne ke bajaye similarly structured reasoning produce karna seekhta hai.

Har example ko CoT format ki zaroorat nahi hai — "What's the normal range for blood pressure" jaise simple factual questions par elaborate reasoning traces sirf tokens badhayenge, value nahi. Practical mix lagbhag two-thirds standard Q&A aur one-third CoT hai, aur CoT examples complex questions par concentrate hone chahiye — isliye Evol-Instruct ka kaam pehle karna achha hai. Chhote models ki limitations bhi yaad rakho: easy questions ke liye chhota local model, difficult ke liye bada hosted model — hybrid approach behtar hai.

Hallucination detection — dusra model verifier bane

Teacher model hallucinate karega — fabricated drug names, nonexistent guidelines, galat dosages — aur medical data me ye fabrications plausible-sounding hone ki wajah se khaas taur par dangerous hain. Practical first line of defense: dusre model ko verifier banao. Verification prompt question-answer pair ko accuracy ke liye review karta hai — fabricated drug names, incorrect dosages ya treatment protocols, outdated ya contradicted guidance, aur misleading ya harmful claims check karta hai — aur temperature 0.1 par chalaya jaata hai, consistent verification ke liye.

Ye meaningful amount pakad leta hai — practice me lagbhag 10% dataset review ke liye flag hota hai, high hit rate of true errors ke saath. Kuch false positives bhi honge, aur sab kuch capture nahi hoga — foolproof se bahut door hai. Book khud kehta hai ki learning ke liye same chhote model se verify karna shortcut hai; real-world me bada hosted model ya independently trained verifier use karna chahiye, aur medical jaise important scenario me human expert review ka koi substitute nahi hai. Bade aur smart models ko checker banana mehenga hai, lekin long run me payoff deta hai.

Diversity checks — n-gram overlap ratio

Models repetitive patterns me gir jaate hain, aur ye numbers me pakda ja sakta hai. Unique n-gram ratio bigrams aur trigrams gin kar batata hai ki kitne unique hain: ratio 1.0 ke paas matlab text rarely phrase repeat karta hai, low ratio matlab wahi word sequences baar-baar aa rahe hain. Rule of thumb: 0.7 se neeche score red flag hai — teacher same phrases heavily reuse kar raha hai. Tab temperature upar badhao aur seed prompts me aur variation add karo. Honest reporting: book ke hosted datasets me se GPT-OSS-120B wala dataset khud is par low score karta tha — ye book me honestly report kiya gaya hai, aur download me consistency ke liye waisa hi rakha gaya hai.

Filtering — 20% khona achha hai

Final filter simple hai: verification me inaccurate paya gaya to hatao; answer 200 se 2,000 characters ke beech na ho to hatao; answer me condition ka naam hi na aaye (teacher ne seed ko ignore kar diya) to hatao. Expect karo ki quality filtering me lagbhag 20% examples kho jayenge — aur ye achhi baat hai, 1,000 polluted samples se 800 high-quality samples behtar hain. Agar loss 30% se zyada hai, to generation prompts improve karo. Agar 5% se kam hai, to quality check bahut lax hai — wapas jao aur sab kuch dobara check karo. Good results par kabhi blind trust mat karo!

Mixing real aur synthetic data — teen strategies

  • Uniform mix: 150 real + 850 synthetic ko randomly shuffle karke 1,000 ka combined dataset banao. Kaam karta hai, lekin model synthetic data ki taraf bias ho sakta hai kyunki woh zyada hain.
  • Upsampling real data 3–4x: 150 real examples ko 3–4 baar repeat karo, to combined set me real data ki representation lagbhag 40% ho jaati hai — model ko real patterns par anchor milta hai, synthetic ki breadth bhi rehti hai.
  • Curriculum training (book ki recommendation): pehle poore synthetic dataset par fine-tune karo (broad competence), phir dusri pass sirf real data par karo (real-world patterns par anchor). Two-stage approach zyada time leta hai, lekin generally behtar results deta hai — pehla stage classroom ki theoretical learning, dusra stage field me internship.

Verification step highly domain-specific hai, jabki generation generic ho sakti hai — medical verification prompt code generation ya legal documents wale se bilkul alag dikhega. Verification me engineering effort invest karna hi aapki quality ka source hai.

Yaad rakho: Generate karna fast aur sasta hai — verify, filter aur curate karna hi asli engineering hai. 20% khona achha hai, 5% se kam khona warning sign hai.

06Chapter 6 · Preparing Your Dataset for Fine-Tuning

Preparing Your Dataset for Fine-Tuning

Chapter 5 tak tumhare paas ek medical Q&A dataset tha — sawaal aur jawab, saaf-suthre records me. Lekin ek language model text par train nahi hota, woh tokens par train hota hai, aur woh tokens ek template ke hisaab se arrange hote hain jo model ne apni training me dekha tha. Agar tum apna data us template se alag format me doge, to model tumhare mehnat se banaye hue data ko noise samjhega. Is chapter ka kaam hai wahi gap bharna: raw Q&A pairs ko us exact token sequence me badalna jo fine-tuning framework expect karta hai.

Ye gap sirf file format ka nahi hai. Har bada fine-tuning framework — chahe woh ek hosted fine-tuning API ho, ya Hugging Face ka TRL, Axolotl ya Unsloth — data ki structure ke baare me specific expectations rakhta hai. Usse bhi important baat: jis model ko tum fine-tune kar rahe ho, woh pretraining aur instruction tuning ke dauraan ek specific template par train hua tha — special tokens aur role markers ka ek pattern jo batata hai ki instruction kahan shuru hoti hai, jawab kahan se shuru hota hai, aur ek turn kahan khatam hota hai. Fine-tune karte waqt tumhe wahi template exactly reproduce karna hota hai.

Galat format ki keemat

Bahut se fine-tuning attempts kagaz par sahi lagte hain — data achha hai, hyperparameters reasonable hain — lekin result disappointing hota hai, kyunki format halka sa galat tha. Model ne apna training budget task seekhne ke bajaye format correct karne me kharch kar diya. Isliye data ko human-readable form se model ke templatized form me badalne wala translation layer is poori process ka sabse crucial hissa hai.

Chapter ka safar

  • Do paradigms: completion aur chat — aur kyun modern instruction-tuned models ke liye chat format sahi choice hai.
  • Chat templates: Jinja2 templates jo messages ko exact token sequence me render karte hain, aur har model family ka apna alag template kyun hota hai.
  • Conversion: Alpaca-style records ko messages format me badalna, 85 / 10 / 5 split, aur TRL ke SFTTrainer se pehli training.
  • Loss masking aur frameworks: sirf assistant ke tokens par loss compute karna, Axolotl aur Unsloth se pipeline test karna, aur splits aur validation ko sahi tareeke se karna.

Running example wahi hai jo poori book me chal raha hai: Gemma 4 par medical Q&A fine-tune, jiska dataset Hugging Face par author/synthdata naam se hosted hai. Har record me instruction, input, output aur metadata fields hain — jaise category, condition aur question type. Real world me tumhara data zyada verified aur real data ke saath mix hoga, lekin structurally yehi starting point hai.

Yaad rakho: model ko data nahi, template ke hisaab se arrange kiye hue tokens milte hain. Format ko halke me lena matlab hai training budget ko format sikhane me barbaad karna, task sikhane ke bajaye.

%pip install -U "datasets>=5.0" transformers trl accelerate peft torchao -q
# torchao is included because an outdated copy (common in shared
# environments) causes an ImportError when transformers loads the model.
# If this cell upgrades anything, restart the kernel before continuing.
# Gemma is gated on the Hugging Face Hub — log in with a token that has
# accepted the license on the model page.
from huggingface_hub import notebook_login
notebook_login()
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

MODEL_NAME = "google/gemma-4-E4B-it"

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_NAME)

demo_messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful medical assistant."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "What are the warning signs of high blood pressure?"},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "High blood pressure rarely causes noticeable symptoms..."},
]

print(tokenizer.apply_chat_template(demo_messages, tokenize=False,
                                    add_generation_prompt=False))
from datasets import load_dataset

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a board-certified physician providing educational \
medical information. Your answers are accurate, practical, and always recommend \
consulting a healthcare provider for personalized advice."""


def to_prompt_completion(example: dict) -> dict:
    user_content = example["instruction"]
    if example.get("input", "").strip():
        user_content = f"{example['instruction']}\n\n{example['input']}"
    return {
        "prompt": [
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_content},
        ],
        "completion": [
            {"role": "assistant", "content": example["output"]},
        ],
    }


raw = load_dataset("[Name]/synthdata", split="train")
dataset = raw.map(to_prompt_completion, remove_columns=raw.column_names)
print(dataset)
# Extract 85% for training, leaving 15% as a remainder
train_and_remainder = dataset.train_test_split(test_size=0.15, seed=42)
train_set = train_and_remainder["train"]
remainder = train_and_remainder["test"]

# Split the 15% remainder: 10% validation, 5% test (5% is 1/3 of 15%)
val_test_split = remainder.train_test_split(test_size=1 / 3, seed=42)
val_set = val_test_split["train"]
test_set = val_test_split["test"]

print(f"train: {len(train_set)}, validation: {len(val_set)}, test: {len(test_set)}")
MAX_TOKENS = 2048

lengths = []
for example in train_set:
    formatted = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
        example["prompt"] + example["completion"],
        tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=False,
    )
    lengths.append(len(tokenizer.encode(formatted)))

s = sorted(lengths)
pick = lambda p: s[min(int(len(s) * p), len(s) - 1)]
over = sum(1 for n in lengths if n > MAX_TOKENS)
print(f"Token length — p50: {pick(0.50)}, p90: {pick(0.90)}, "
      f"p99: {pick(0.99)}, max: {s[-1]}")
print(f"Over limit ({MAX_TOKENS} tokens): {over}")
def validate_example(example):
    """Returns (is_valid, list_of_issues) for one prompt-completion example."""
    issues = []
    messages = example.get("prompt", []) + example.get("completion", [])

    # The messages list should not be empty
    if not messages:
        return False, ["messages list is empty"]

    # The last message should be the model's turn
    if messages[-1]["role"] not in ("assistant", "model"):
        issues.append(f"last role is '{messages[-1]['role']}', expected the model's turn")

    # At least one message should come from the user
    if not any(m["role"] == "user" for m in messages):
        issues.append("no user message in conversation")

    # There should be no empty messages
    for i, m in enumerate(messages):
        if not m.get("content", "").strip():
            issues.append(f"message {i} (role={m.get('role')}) is empty")

    # The template must apply without throwing
    try:
        tokenizer.apply_chat_template(messages, tokenize=False)
    except Exception as e:
        issues.append(f"chat template failed: {e}")

    return len(issues) == 0, issues


valid = 0
for i, example in enumerate(train_set):
    ok, issues = validate_example(example)
    if ok:
        valid += 1
    else:
        print(f"Example {i} FAILED: {'; '.join(issues)}")

print(f"Valid examples: {valid}/{len(train_set)}")
example = train_set[0]

prompt_text = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    example["prompt"], tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True)
full_text = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    example["prompt"] + example["completion"],
    tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=False)

prompt_ids = tokenizer.encode(prompt_text, add_special_tokens=False)
full_ids = tokenizer.encode(full_text, add_special_tokens=False)
labels = [-100] * len(prompt_ids) + full_ids[len(prompt_ids):]

for token_id, label in zip(full_ids, labels):
    status = "TRAIN" if label != -100 else "MASK "
    print(f"{status} | {tokenizer.decode([token_id])!r}")
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    MODEL_NAME,
    torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
    device_map="auto",
)
# OPTIONAL (recommended on a single GPU): add a LoRA adapter.
# Trains ~1% of the parameters — see Chapter 7 for how this works.
from peft import LoraConfig

peft_config = LoraConfig(
    r=16,
    lora_alpha=32,
    lora_dropout=0.05,
    target_modules="all-linear",
    task_type="CAUSAL_LM",
)
# If you skip this cell, set peft_config = None before the trainer cell.
from trl import SFTTrainer, SFTConfig

config = SFTConfig(
    output_dir="checkpoints/medical-qa-gemma4-v1",
    num_train_epochs=3,
    per_device_train_batch_size=4,
    gradient_accumulation_steps=4,
    learning_rate=2e-4,          # LoRA rate; use ~2e-5 for a full fine-tune
    warmup_ratio=0.05,
    logging_steps=10,
    eval_strategy="steps",
    eval_steps=100,
    save_strategy="steps",
    save_steps=200,
    bf16=True,
    max_length=2048,
    completion_only_loss=True,   # mask the prompt; train on the answer
    # max_steps=20,              # uncomment for a quick smoke test
)

trainer = SFTTrainer(
    model=model,
    args=config,
    train_dataset=train_set,
    eval_dataset=val_set,
    processing_class=tokenizer,
    peft_config=peft_config,     # None for a full fine-tune
)

trainer.train()
test_example = test_set[0]
print("QUESTION:", test_example["prompt"][-1]["content"], "\n")

inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    test_example["prompt"],
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    return_tensors="pt",
).to(model.device)

with torch.no_grad():
    output = model.generate(inputs, max_new_tokens=400)

print(tokenizer.decode(output[0][inputs.shape[1]:], skip_special_tokens=True))
trainer.save_model("medical-qa-gemma4-final")
tokenizer.save_pretrained("medical-qa-gemma4-final")

"""
Chapter 6: Preparing Your Dataset for Fine Tuning
=================================================
Section: Using OpenAI's Templates

Converts the Alpaca-format synthetic dataset from Chapter 5 into the
OpenAI fine-tuning 'messages' format — one JSON object per line, each
with a messages list of role/content dictionaries. You never write the
special tokens (<|im_start|> etc.) yourself; the API applies the template.

The data is pulled from the book's hosted dataset on the Hugging Face
Hub (https://huggingface.co/datasets/[Name]/synthdata), so you can
run this without having generated your own data in Chapter 5. If you
DID generate your own, point DATASET_NAME at your local JSONL instead:
    load_dataset("json", data_files="medical_qa_synthetic.jsonl", split="train")

Run this BEFORE chapter06_trl_training.py: it writes the three files
that script (and the chapter's 85/10/5 split guidance) expects:

    data/formatted/medical_qa_openai.jsonl   (85% — training)
    data/formatted/medical_qa_val.jsonl      (10% — validation)
    data/formatted/medical_qa_test.jsonl     ( 5% — held-out test)

After converting, validate the output with the script in OpenAI's
cookbook: the Chat_finetuning_data_prep.ipynb notebook at
https://github.com/openai/openai-cookbook — the most common error it
catches is an assistant message that's empty after stripping whitespace.
"""

import json
import random
from pathlib import Path

from datasets import load_dataset

DATASET_NAME = "[Name]/synthdata"

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a board-certified physician providing educational \
medical information. Your answers are accurate, practical, and always recommend \
consulting a healthcare provider for personalized advice."""


def alpaca_to_messages(example: dict) -> dict | None:
    """Convert one Alpaca record to the messages format, or None to skip."""
    # Skip examples with an empty output — these slip through when
    # the teacher model returned a blank response (see Chapter 5)
    if not example.get("output", "").strip():
        return None

    messages = [
        {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
        {"role": "user", "content": example["instruction"]},
        {"role": "assistant", "content": example["output"]},
    ]

    # Include input field if present and non-empty
    if example.get("input", "").strip():
        messages[1]["content"] = (
            f"{example['instruction']}\n\n{example['input']}"
        )
    return {"messages": messages}


def alpaca_to_openai(train_path: Path, val_path: Path,
                     test_path: Path) -> None:
    """Convert the hosted Alpaca-format dataset to OpenAI fine-tuning
    JSONL, split 85/10/5 into train/validation/test files."""
    data = load_dataset(DATASET_NAME, split="train")
    converted, skipped = [], 0
    for example in data:
        record = alpaca_to_messages(example)
        if record is None:
            skipped += 1
        else:
            converted.append(record)

    # Shuffle with a fixed seed so the split is reproducible, then
    # cut 85% / 10% / 5% (see 'Splitting and Validating your Dataset')
    random.Random(42).shuffle(converted)
    n = len(converted)
    train_end = int(n * 0.85)
    val_end = int(n * 0.95)
    splits = [
        (train_path, converted[:train_end]),
        (val_path, converted[train_end:val_end]),
        (test_path, converted[val_end:]),
    ]

    for path, records in splits:
        path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        with open(path, "w") as outfile:
            for record in records:
                outfile.write(json.dumps(record) + "\n")
        print(f"Wrote {len(records)} examples to {path}")

    if skipped:
        print(f"Skipped {skipped} examples with empty outputs — "
              f"check your Chapter 5 filtering step!")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    alpaca_to_openai(
        Path("data/formatted/medical_qa_openai.jsonl"),
        Path("data/formatted/medical_qa_val.jsonl"),
        Path("data/formatted/medical_qa_test.jsonl"),
    )
chapter06_axolotl_smoke_test.yaml — Config file  ·  GitHub ↗ 
# Chapter 6: Preparing Your Dataset for Fine Tuning
# Section: Other Frameworks — Axolotl
#
# A smoke-test configuration for the medical Q&A dataset: QLoRA on
# Gemma 4 E4B, capped at 20 steps. Designed to verify the data
# pipeline, not to produce a good model. Works on a free Google Colab
# GPU instance.
#
# NOTE: Axolotl calls CUDA-specific functions at startup — it won't run
# on a Mac or a CPU-only machine. You can write and validate this file
# anywhere, but run it on a CUDA box:
#
#   axolotl train chapter06_axolotl_smoke_test.yaml
#
# Gemma is gated on the Hugging Face Hub: accept the license on the
# model page and log in (hf auth login) before running.

base_model: google/gemma-4-E4B-it
model_type: AutoModelForCausalLM
tokenizer_type: AutoTokenizer

datasets:
  # Point 'path' at your messages-format JSONL from this chapter
  - path: data/formatted/medical_qa_train.jsonl
    ds_type: json
    # 'chat_template' applies the model's native chat template to the
    # messages field. Other supported types include alpaca, sharegpt,
    # and completion.
    type: chat_template
    split: train

dataset_prepared_path: prepared_data
val_set_size: 0.05

output_dir: checkpoints/smoke-test

sequence_len: 1024
# Axolotl's equivalent of loss masking: mask all non-assistant tokens.
# For instruction tuning, ALWAYS set this to false!
train_on_inputs: false

# QLoRA config — the base model is loaded in 4-bit, so this 8B model
# trains comfortably within a 16GB GPU (see Chapter 7 for how QLoRA works)
adapter: qlora
load_in_4bit: true
lora_r: 16
lora_alpha: 32
lora_dropout: 0.05
lora_target_linear: true

micro_batch_size: 2
gradient_accumulation_steps: 4
max_steps: 20
learning_rate: 2e-4
warmup_steps: 5
optimizer: adamw_torch
lr_scheduler: cosine

bf16: auto
tf32: false

logging_steps: 5
eval_steps: 10
save_steps: 20
chapter06_chat_templates.py — Python script  ·  GitHub ↗ 
"""
Chapter 6: Preparing Your Dataset for Fine Tuning
=================================================
Section: Chat Templates — Using Templates with HuggingFace

Demonstrates how a model's built-in chat template turns a structured
messages list into the flat, special-token-delimited string the model
actually consumes. Uses tokenize=False so you can see the intermediate
string — the single most useful debugging trick in this chapter.
"""

from transformers import AutoTokenizer

# Load the tokenizer for the model you're fine-tuning.
# Swap in any model to see its template — e.g. "meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct",
# "Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct", "google/gemma-3-1b-it".
MODEL_NAME = "openai/gpt-oss-20b"

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_NAME)

messages = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful medical assistant providing "
     "educational information. Always recommend consulting a healthcare provider."},
    {"role": "user", "content": "What are the warning signs of high blood pressure?"},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "High blood pressure rarely causes noticeable "
     "symptoms, which is why it's often called the silent killer..."},
]

# tokenize=False gives you the formatted string before tokenization
formatted = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    messages,
    tokenize=False,
    add_generation_prompt=False,
)
print("=== Formatted string (training form: full assistant turn included) ===")
print(formatted)

# add_generation_prompt=True appends the OPENING of the assistant turn with no
# closing token — the signal for the model to keep generating. This is what
# you want at INFERENCE time, never in training data (where the full
# assistant response is already present).
inference_messages = messages[:-1]  # drop the assistant answer
formatted_for_inference = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    inference_messages,
    tokenize=False,
    add_generation_prompt=True,
)
print("\n=== Formatted string (inference form: open assistant turn) ===")
print(formatted_for_inference)

# With tokenize=True you get the token IDs that are ready for training.
token_ids = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    messages,
    tokenize=True,
    add_generation_prompt=False,
)
print(f"\nToken count after tokenization: {len(token_ids)}")

# Bonus: the template itself is just a Jinja2 string shipped with the
# tokenizer. Print it to see the source of truth for this model's format.
print("\n=== The model's raw Jinja2 chat template ===")
print(tokenizer.chat_template)

chapter06_loss_masking.py — Python script  ·  GitHub ↗ 
"""
Chapter 6: Preparing Your Dataset for Fine Tuning
=================================================
Section: Loss Masking

Without masking, the loss is computed over EVERY token — system prompt,
instruction, and role markers included — so part of your training budget
is spent teaching the model to reproduce questions. Loss masking sets
the labels for non-response tokens to -100 (PyTorch's 'ignore this token
in the loss' convention) so the gradient comes only from the answer.

NOTE ON TRL VERSIONS: older TRL provided DataCollatorForCompletionOnlyLM
for this; it was removed in recent versions. The modern approach is
built into SFTTrainer: structure the data as PROMPT-COMPLETION pairs and
set completion_only_loss=True in SFTConfig. Everything in the prompt is
masked; only completion tokens produce gradient.

This script converts the Alpaca data to prompt-completion form, shows
the trainer configuration, then reproduces the masking locally so you
can inspect it: every token prints with TRAIN or MASK status. Only the
assistant's response tokens should say TRAIN.
"""

from datasets import load_dataset
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

MODEL_NAME = "openai/gpt-oss-20b"

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a board-certified physician providing educational \
medical information. Your answers are accurate, practical, and always recommend \
consulting a healthcare provider for personalized advice."""

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_NAME)


# ── Convert Alpaca records to conversational prompt-completion ───────
# The 'prompt' holds everything the model reads as context (system +
# user turns); the 'completion' holds only the assistant's answer.
# With completion_only_loss=True, SFTTrainer masks the whole prompt.
def to_prompt_completion(example: dict) -> dict:
    user_content = example["instruction"]
    if example.get("input", "").strip():
        user_content = f"{example['instruction']}\n\n{example['input']}"
    return {
        "prompt": [
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_content},
        ],
        "completion": [
            {"role": "assistant", "content": example["output"]},
        ],
    }


# Pull the book's hosted dataset from the Hugging Face Hub
raw = load_dataset("[Name]/synthdata", split="train")
pc_dataset = raw.map(to_prompt_completion, remove_columns=raw.column_names)

# ── The training setup (see chapter06_trl_training.py for the rest) ──
#
# from trl import SFTTrainer, SFTConfig
#
# config = SFTConfig(
#     output_dir="checkpoints/medical-qa-v1",
#     completion_only_loss=True,   # mask the prompt; train on the answer
#     max_length=2048,
#     ...
# )
# trainer = SFTTrainer(
#     model=model,
#     args=config,
#     train_dataset=pc_dataset,
#     processing_class=tokenizer,
# )

# ── Verify the masking by reproducing it for one example ─────────────
# This mirrors what the trainer does internally: tokenize the rendered
# prompt, tokenize prompt+completion, and label the prompt tokens -100.
if __name__ == "__main__":
    example = pc_dataset[0]

    prompt_text = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
        example["prompt"], tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True,
    )
    full_text = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
        example["prompt"] + example["completion"],
        tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=False,
    )

    prompt_ids = tokenizer.encode(prompt_text, add_special_tokens=False)
    full_ids = tokenizer.encode(full_text, add_special_tokens=False)

    labels = [-100] * len(prompt_ids) + full_ids[len(prompt_ids):]

    # Print the token / label pairs
    for token_id, label in zip(full_ids, labels):
        token = tokenizer.decode([token_id])
        status = "TRAIN" if label != -100 else "MASK "
        print(f"{status} | {repr(token)}")

    # If you see TRAIN on system prompt or instruction tokens, the
    # prompt/completion boundary is wrong — check that your prompt list
    # ends with the user turn and the completion holds only the answer.

chapter06_split_and_validate.py — Python script  ·  GitHub ↗ 
"""
Chapter 6: Preparing Your Dataset for Fine Tuning
=================================================
Sections: Splitting and Validating your Dataset / Format Validation /
          Inspecting Tokenized Examples

This is the full validation code referenced in the chapter ("much too
long to put into print"). It:

  1. Splits the dataset 85/10/5 into train/validation/test
  2. Validates every example against Gemma-oriented format rules
  3. Reports token-length percentiles (p50/p90/p99/max)
  4. Lets you eyeball individual formatted examples

Expected output looks like:

    Valid examples: 580/580
    Token length — p50: 435, p90: 510, p99: 560, max: 700
    Over limit (2048 tokens): 0
"""

from datasets import load_dataset
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

MODEL_NAME = "google/gemma-4-E4B-it"
MAX_TOKENS = 2048

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a board-certified physician providing educational \
medical information. Your answers are accurate, practical, and always recommend \
consulting a healthcare provider for personalized advice."""

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_NAME)


# ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Template helper for models without a standalone system role
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

def _apply_template_safe(tokenizer, messages, **kwargs):
    """Apply the chat template, folding the system message into the
    first user turn for models whose template rejects a standalone
    system role. (Gemma 4 accepts the system role natively, so for our
    model the fallback never triggers — but earlier Gemma generations
    and some other families need it, so it's a useful general tool.)"""
    try:
        return tokenizer.apply_chat_template(messages, **kwargs)
    except Exception:
        if messages and messages[0]["role"] == "system":
            system = messages[0]["content"]
            rest = [dict(m) for m in messages[1:]]
            if rest and rest[0]["role"] == "user":
                rest[0]["content"] = f"{system}\n\n{rest[0]['content']}"
                return tokenizer.apply_chat_template(rest, **kwargs)
        raise  # a different problem — let the caller see it


# ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Format validation rules (a good starting point for any model)
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

def normalize(example: dict) -> list | None:
    """Accept either a 'messages' key or both 'instruction' and
    'output' keys (Alpaca). Anything else fails (returns None)."""
    if "messages" in example:
        return example["messages"]
    if "instruction" in example and "output" in example:
        user_content = example["instruction"]
        if example.get("input", "").strip():
            user_content = f"{user_content}\n\n{example['input']}"
        return [
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_content},
            {"role": "assistant", "content": example["output"]},
        ]
    return None


def validate_example(example: dict) -> tuple[bool, list, int]:
    """Returns (is_valid, list_of_issues, token_count)."""
    issues = []
    token_count = 0

    messages = normalize(example)
    if messages is None:
        return False, ["needs 'messages', or both 'instruction' and 'output'"], 0

    # The messages list should not be empty
    if not messages:
        return False, ["messages list is empty"], 0

    # The last message should be the model's turn
    # (Gemma calls the assistant role 'model'; messages-format data
    # uses 'assistant' and the template maps it — accept either)
    if messages[-1]["role"] not in ("assistant", "model"):
        issues.append(f"last message role is '{messages[-1]['role']}', "
                      f"expected the model's turn")

    # At least one message should come from the user
    if not any(m["role"] == "user" for m in messages):
        issues.append("no user message in conversation")

    # There should be no empty messages
    for i, m in enumerate(messages):
        if not m.get("content", "").strip():
            issues.append(f"message {i} (role={m.get('role')}) is empty")

    # The template must apply without throwing, and the formatted
    # example must fit within the model's maximum token length
    try:
        formatted = _apply_template_safe(tokenizer, messages, tokenize=False)
        token_count = len(tokenizer.encode(formatted))
        if token_count > MAX_TOKENS:
            issues.append(f"too long: {token_count} > {MAX_TOKENS} tokens")
    except Exception as e:
        issues.append(f"chat template failed: {e}")

    return len(issues) == 0, issues, token_count


# ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Token-length statistics
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

def length_percentiles(lengths: list) -> dict:
    """p50/p90/p99/max over token lengths. A big gap between p90 and
    p99 flags a handful of unusually long examples — a red flag."""
    s = sorted(lengths)
    pick = lambda p: s[min(int(len(s) * p), len(s) - 1)] if s else 0
    return {"p50": pick(0.50), "p90": pick(0.90),
            "p99": pick(0.99), "max": s[-1] if s else 0}


# ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Eyeball inspection of individual examples
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

def inspect_example(dataset, tokenizer, index: int = 0) -> None:
    """Print a tokenized example with its formatted string."""
    example = dataset[index]
    messages = normalize(example)

    print(f"=== Example {index} ===")
    for msg in messages:
        print(f"\n[{msg['role'].upper()}]")
        print(msg["content"])

    # Show the full formatted string as the model sees it
    formatted = _apply_template_safe(tokenizer, messages, tokenize=False)
    print(f"\n=== Formatted String ({len(formatted)} chars) ===")
    print(formatted)

    # Show the token count
    tokens = tokenizer.encode(formatted)
    print(f"\nTotal tokens: {len(tokens)}")


# ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Load, split 85/10/5, validate, report
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # 1. Load the raw dataset into 'all_data' from the book's hosted
    # dataset on the Hugging Face Hub. (To use your own Chapter 5
    # output instead: load_dataset("json",
    #     data_files={"data": "medical_qa_synthetic.jsonl"}, split="data"))
    all_data = load_dataset("[Name]/synthdata", split="train")

    # 2. Extract 85% for Training, leaving 15% as a remainder
    train_and_remainder = all_data.train_test_split(test_size=0.15, seed=42)
    train_set = train_and_remainder["train"]
    remainder = train_and_remainder["test"]

    # 3. Split the 15% remainder: 10% for Validation, 5% for Test
    # (Since 5% is 1/3 of the 15% remainder, we use test_size=1/3)
    val_test_split = remainder.train_test_split(test_size=1 / 3, seed=42)
    val_set = val_test_split["train"]
    test_set = val_test_split["test"]

    print(f"Split sizes — train: {len(train_set)}, "
          f"validation: {len(val_set)}, test: {len(test_set)}")

    # NOTE: this is a naive random split. With synthetic data, near-
    # duplicate seeds (e.g. 'asthma / treatment options') can land in
    # both train and test, inflating your generalization estimate. If
    # that happens, split by category instead, putting whole categories
    # into train or test.

    # 4. Validate every example in the training set
    valid_count = 0
    lengths = []
    over_limit = 0
    for i in range(len(train_set)):
        ok, issues, token_count = validate_example(train_set[i])
        lengths.append(token_count)
        if token_count > MAX_TOKENS:
            over_limit += 1
        if ok:
            valid_count += 1
        else:
            print(f"Example {i} FAILED: {'; '.join(issues)}")

    p = length_percentiles(lengths)
    print(f"\nValid examples: {valid_count}/{len(train_set)}")
    print(f"Token length — p50: {p['p50']}, p90: {p['p90']}, "
          f"p99: {p['p99']}, max: {p['max']}")
    print(f"Over limit ({MAX_TOKENS} tokens): {over_limit}")

    # 5. Spot-check a few examples — beginning, middle, and end
    for i in [0, len(train_set) // 2, len(train_set) - 1]:
        inspect_example(train_set, tokenizer, i)
        print()

"""
Chapter 6: Preparing Your Dataset for Fine Tuning
=================================================
Sections: Formatting for TRL / Using Alpaca with SFTTrainer

A complete TRL training run on the medical Q&A data. Two paths to the
'messages' format SFTTrainer expects:

  1. Load a pre-converted OpenAI-format JSONL (see
     chapter06_alpaca_to_openai.py), or
  2. Convert the raw Alpaca-format JSONL on the fly with
     alpaca_to_messages() below.

SFTTrainer applies the model's native chat template automatically,
using whatever tokenizer you pass — you never hand-format the special
tokens.

NOTE: gpt-oss-20b needs a serious GPU to fine-tune. For a smoke test of
your data pipeline on smaller hardware, swap MODEL_NAME for something
small (e.g. "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct") — the code is identical.
"""

from datasets import load_dataset
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
from trl import SFTTrainer, SFTConfig

MODEL_NAME = "openai/gpt-oss-20b"

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a board-certified physician providing educational \
medical information. Your answers are accurate, practical, and always recommend \
consulting a healthcare provider for personalized advice."""


def alpaca_to_messages(example: dict) -> dict:
    """Convert a single Alpaca record to the messages format SFTTrainer expects."""
    user_content = example["instruction"]
    if example.get("input", "").strip():
        user_content = f"{example['instruction']}\n\n{example['input']}"
    return {
        "messages": [
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_content},
            {"role": "assistant", "content": example["output"]},
        ]
    }


# ── Load model and tokenizer ─────────────────────────────────────────
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_NAME)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(MODEL_NAME)

# ── Path 1: load a dataset already in messages format ────────────────
dataset = load_dataset("json", data_files={
    "train": "data/formatted/medical_qa_openai.jsonl",
    "validation": "data/formatted/medical_qa_val.jsonl",
})

# ── Path 2 (alternative): convert the hosted Alpaca data on the fly ──
# Uncomment to pull the book's dataset straight from the Hugging Face
# Hub (https://huggingface.co/datasets/[Name]/synthdata) instead.
# Note this doesn't split into train/validation — see
# chapter06_split_and_validate.py.
#
# raw = load_dataset("[Name]/synthdata", split="train")
# converted = raw.map(alpaca_to_messages, remove_columns=raw.column_names)
# split = converted.train_test_split(test_size=0.1, seed=42)
# dataset = {"train": split["train"], "validation": split["test"]}

# ── Configure and run the trainer ────────────────────────────────────
config = SFTConfig(
    output_dir="checkpoints/medical-qa-v1",
    num_train_epochs=3,
    per_device_train_batch_size=4,
    gradient_accumulation_steps=4,
    learning_rate=2e-5,
    warmup_ratio=0.05,
    logging_steps=10,
    eval_strategy="steps",
    eval_steps=100,
    save_strategy="steps",
    save_steps=200,
    bf16=True,               # Use bfloat16 if your GPU supports it
    max_length=2048,
)

trainer = SFTTrainer(
    model=model,
    args=config,
    train_dataset=dataset["train"],
    eval_dataset=dataset["validation"],
    processing_class=tokenizer,
)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    trainer.train()

"""
Chapter 6: Preparing Your Dataset for Fine Tuning
=================================================
Sections: Formatting for TRL / Using Alpaca with SFTTrainer

A complete TRL training run on the medical Q&A data. Two paths to the
'messages' format SFTTrainer expects:

  1. Load a pre-converted OpenAI-format JSONL (see
     chapter06_alpaca_to_openai.py), or
  2. Convert the raw Alpaca-format JSONL on the fly with
     alpaca_to_messages() below.

SFTTrainer applies the model's native chat template automatically,
using whatever tokenizer you pass — you never hand-format the special
tokens.

This version uses Gemma 4 E4B ("effective 4B": 8B total parameters,
~4.5B effective via per-layer embeddings). Its chat template accepts
the system role in our messages data natively — no folding into the
user turn needed, unlike Gemma 2/3. A full fine-tune of an 8B model
still wants a data-center GPU; for consumer hardware, add LoRA (see
Chapter 7) or use the Unsloth variant of this script.
"""

from datasets import load_dataset
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
from trl import SFTTrainer, SFTConfig

MODEL_NAME = "google/gemma-4-E4B-it"

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a board-certified physician providing educational \
medical information. Your answers are accurate, practical, and always recommend \
consulting a healthcare provider for personalized advice."""


def alpaca_to_messages(example: dict) -> dict:
    """Convert a single Alpaca record to the messages format SFTTrainer expects."""
    user_content = example["instruction"]
    if example.get("input", "").strip():
        user_content = f"{example['instruction']}\n\n{example['input']}"
    return {
        "messages": [
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_content},
            {"role": "assistant", "content": example["output"]},
        ]
    }


# ── Load model and tokenizer ─────────────────────────────────────────
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_NAME)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(MODEL_NAME)

# ── Path 1: load a dataset already in messages format ────────────────
dataset = load_dataset("json", data_files={
    "train": "data/formatted/medical_qa_openai.jsonl",
    "validation": "data/formatted/medical_qa_val.jsonl",
})

# ── Path 2 (alternative): convert the hosted Alpaca data on the fly ──
# Uncomment to pull the book's dataset straight from the Hugging Face
# Hub (https://huggingface.co/datasets/[Name]/synthdata) instead.
# Note this doesn't split into train/validation — see
# chapter06_split_and_validate.py.
#
# raw = load_dataset("[Name]/synthdata", split="train")
# converted = raw.map(alpaca_to_messages, remove_columns=raw.column_names)
# split = converted.train_test_split(test_size=0.1, seed=42)
# dataset = {"train": split["train"], "validation": split["test"]}

# ── Configure and run the trainer ────────────────────────────────────
config = SFTConfig(
    output_dir="checkpoints/medical-qa-gemma4-v1",
    num_train_epochs=3,
    per_device_train_batch_size=4,
    gradient_accumulation_steps=4,
    learning_rate=2e-5,
    warmup_ratio=0.05,
    logging_steps=10,
    eval_strategy="steps",
    eval_steps=100,
    save_strategy="steps",
    save_steps=200,
    bf16=True,               # Use bfloat16 if your GPU supports it
    max_length=2048,
)

trainer = SFTTrainer(
    model=model,
    args=config,
    train_dataset=dataset["train"],
    eval_dataset=dataset["validation"],
    processing_class=tokenizer,
)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    trainer.train()
chapter06_unsloth_training.py — Python script  ·  GitHub ↗ 
"""
Chapter 6: Preparing Your Dataset for Fine Tuning
=================================================
Section: Other Frameworks — Unsloth

Speed- and memory-optimized fine-tuning of Gemma 4 E4B on the medical
Q&A data. With 4-bit loading, the 8B-parameter model works on a free
Google Colab T4 instance (16GB VRAM). Unsloth's FastLanguageModel is a
drop-in replacement for the HuggingFace loading step; the SFTTrainer
interface is the same as TRL.

Gemma is gated on the Hugging Face Hub — accept the license on the
model page and log in (hf auth login) first.
"""

from datasets import load_dataset
from trl import SFTTrainer, SFTConfig
from unsloth import FastLanguageModel
from unsloth.chat_templates import train_on_responses_only

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You are a board-certified physician providing educational \
medical information. Your answers are accurate, practical, and always recommend \
consulting a healthcare provider for personalized advice."""

# ── Unsloth handles the model loading with optimization enabled ──────
model, tokenizer = FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained(
    model_name="google/gemma-4-E4B-it",
    max_seq_length=2048,
    load_in_4bit=True,       # 4-bit quantization — 8B params in ~5GB
)

# ── Apply LoRA — covered in detail in Chapter 7 ──────────────────────
model = FastLanguageModel.get_peft_model(
    model,
    r=16,                        # LoRA rank
    target_modules=["q_proj", "v_proj", "k_proj", "o_proj",
                    "gate_proj", "up_proj", "down_proj"],
    lora_alpha=16,
    lora_dropout=0,
    bias="none",
)


# ── Prepare the data: Alpaca → messages, then split ──────────────────
# Gemma 4 accepts a standalone system role natively (earlier Gemma
# generations did not — they required folding the system prompt into
# the first user turn).
def alpaca_to_messages(example: dict) -> dict:
    user_content = example["instruction"]
    if example.get("input", "").strip():
        user_content = f"{example['instruction']}\n\n{example['input']}"
    return {
        "messages": [
            {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_content},
            {"role": "assistant", "content": example["output"]},
        ]
    }


# Pull the book's hosted dataset from the Hugging Face Hub
raw = load_dataset("[Name]/synthdata", split="train")
dataset = raw.map(alpaca_to_messages, remove_columns=raw.column_names)
split = dataset.train_test_split(test_size=0.1, seed=42)
train_ds, eval_ds = split["train"], split["test"]


# Unsloth's SFTTrainer requires an explicit formatting_func — it does
# not auto-detect the messages format the way vanilla TRL does. We
# apply the tokenizer's template here to produce the formatted string.
# If training fails or the model doesn't learn, look HERE first: the
# output must match the model's expected format exactly.
def formatting_func(example):
    texts = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
        example["messages"],
        tokenize=False,
        add_generation_prompt=False,
    )
    return texts if isinstance(texts, list) else [texts]


# ── The SFTTrainer call is identical to the TRL example ──────────────
trainer = SFTTrainer(
    model=model,
    args=SFTConfig(
        output_dir="checkpoints/medical-qa-unsloth",
        num_train_epochs=3,
        per_device_train_batch_size=4,
        gradient_accumulation_steps=4,
        learning_rate=2e-4,
        fp16=True,
        bf16=False,
        max_length=2048,
    ),
    train_dataset=train_ds,
    eval_dataset=eval_ds,
    processing_class=tokenizer,
    formatting_func=formatting_func,
)

# Loss masking: Unsloth provides train_on_responses_only() as a native
# alternative to TRL's collator approach. Call it after constructing
# the trainer, passing the exact strings that open the instruction and
# response turns in the chat template. These are GEMMA 4's turn tokens —
# earlier Gemma generations used <start_of_turn>user / <start_of_turn>model,
# and using those here would silently mask nothing. Verify against
# print(tokenizer.apply_chat_template(...)) whenever you change models!
trainer = train_on_responses_only(
    trainer,
    instruction_part="<|turn>user\n",
    response_part="<|turn>model\n",
)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    trainer.train()
SOURCESource: Fine-Tuning AI, O'Reilly, Chapter 6 — Preparing Your Dataset for Fine-Tuning
← Previous05.2 · Evol-Instruct, Chain-of-Thought, and Quality Control→ Next06.1 · Completion vs Chat, and Chat Templates
06.1Chapter 6 · Preparing Your Dataset for Fine-Tuning

Completion vs Chat, and Chat Templates

Fine-tuning data aakhir me do forms me se ek leta hai: completion ya chat. Dono ka matlab samajhna zaroori hai, kyunki galat form chunna matlab hai model ko galat cheez sikhana.

Completion format

Completion me ek hi string hoti hai jisme input aur expected output dono hote hain, aur dono ke beech ki boundary sirf text se implicit hoti hai — koi explicit structural marker nahi. Example: prompt ho Answer the following medical question: What are...? aur completion ho High blood pressure rarely causes.... Model seekhta hai ki prompt ko completion se continue kare. Ye kaam karta hai, lekin fragile hai: instruction aur jawab ke beech ki boundary sirf phrasing se define hoti hai, isliye inference time par agar tum thoda sa alag instruction format use karo, to output degrade ho jaata hai.

Chat format — messages

Chat format me data ek sequence of turns hota hai, har turn me ek explicit role aur content hota hai. Roles ka matlab seedha hai: system model ke liye behavioural instructions hai, user insaan ka input hai, aur assistant model ka response hai. Medical Q&A ke liye ek example aisa dikhta hai: system role me You are a medical assistant..., user role me sawaal, aur assistant role me jawab. Ye format aaj ke hosted fine-tuning APIs, Hugging Face TRL aur lagbhag har modern framework me use hota hai. Ye verbose hai, lekin explicit role structure ki wajah se zyada resilient hai — model ek specific prefix string ke bajaye user turn ka jawab dena seekhta hai. Inference time par bhi tum model se usi chat API aur usi role structure se baat karte ho, to training aur inference ka format ek hi rehta hai. Debugging ke liye bhi ye format behtar hai, kyunki conversation ka thread padhna aasan hota hai.

Chat templates: messages se tokens tak

Messages list aur model ko milne wale tokens ke beech ek aur step hai: chat template. Ye ek model-specific Jinja2 template hai jo structured messages ko special tokens ke saath ek flat string me serialize karta hai. Jinja2 Python duniya ka ek templating engine hai — placeholders aur simple logic (loops, if-statements) wale text ko engine real data se bhar deta hai. Chat template wahi machinery use karke messages list par loop karta hai aur har role ko model ke special tokens me lapet kar ek string bana deta hai.

Template zoo — har family ka apna template

  • ChatML: <|im_start|> aur <|im_end|> markers se har role ko wrap karta hai. Ye kai models me use hota hai.
  • Llama: <|start_header_id|> aur <|eot_id|> (end of turn) use karta hai, aur conversation <|begin_of_text|> se shuru hoti hai — koi end marker nahi, kyunki conversation ongoing hoti hai.
  • Mistral: [INST] aur [/INST] se user text ko wrap karta hai. Iske original template me dedicated system message nahi hota — system instructions aam taur par pehle user turn me prepend ki jaati hain.
  • Gemma 4: turn-based approach — <bos> se shuru, phir <|turn> markers, aur role ka naam assistant ke bajaye model hai. Yehi template poori book me use hota hai.

Ye special tokens model ki vocabulary ka hissa hain aur seedhe uske weights me trained hain. Galat template use karna matlab hai galat special tokens — bytes to honge, lekin model unhe samajh nahi payega.

Code me template apply karna

Hugging Face ke tokenizers har supported model ke liye sahi template ship karte hain, to tumhe template string haath se likhne ki zaroorat nahi. tokenizer.apply_chat_template(messages, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=False) call karo aur formatted string mil jaati hai. tokenize=False rakhne se intermediate string milti hai jo debugging ke liye bahut useful hai — training se pehle kuch examples ki strings ko sample karke dekhna best practice hai. add_generation_prompt=True assistant turn ki opening ko bina closing token ke append kar deta hai — ye inference time par chahiye, jab model ko generate karna hai. Training me ise False rakho, kyunki poora assistant response training data me pehle se hai.

Yaad rakho: hamesha wahi template use karo jo tumhare base model se match karta hai. Dusre model ka template use karne se model syntactically sahi text generate karega, lekin unpredictably respond karega — kyunki training data ke special tokens model ke trained tokens se match nahi karte.
SOURCESource: Fine-Tuning AI, O'Reilly, Chapter 6 — Preparing Your Dataset for Fine-Tuning
← Previous06 · Preparing Your Dataset for Fine-Tuning→ Next06.2 · Converting Data and Training with TRL
06.2Chapter 6 · Preparing Your Dataset for Fine-Tuning

Converting Data and Training with TRL

Ab data ko messages format me convert karte hain, use split karte hain, aur TRL ke SFTTrainer se pehli training chalate hain. Ye chapter ka hands-on hissa hai — yahan galti karna sasta hai, training ke baad debug karna mehenga.

Alpaca se messages tak

Book ka data Alpaca style me hai — instruction, input, output fields — jo samajhne aur code karne me aasan hai, aur jise messages format me convert karna straightforward hai. Conversion function ek consistent system prompt jodta hai (ek physician persona jo accurate, practical answers deta hai aur hamesha healthcare provider se consult karne ki salah deta hai), phir instruction aur input (agar khaali nahi hai) ko mila kar user content banata hai, aur output ko assistant content banata hai. Dhyaan do: Alpaca standardized nahi hai — uske multiple variants hain jo ek dusre se compatible nahi hain, to variant chunne me careful raho.

85 / 10 / 5 split

Convert karne ke baad data ko shuffle karke split karo: 85% training, 10% validation, 5% test. Seed 42 use karo taaki split reproducible rahe. Validation set training ke dauraan loss monitor karne aur overfitting detect karne ke liye hai; test set ko training ke baad tak hold back rakho, taaki unseen data par honest performance estimate mile. Code me random.Random(42).shuffle(converted) ke baad teen JSONL files likhi jaati hain: medical_qa_train.jsonl, medical_qa_val.jsonl aur medical_qa_test.jsonl.

Empty-assistant trap

File ko validate karna mat bhoolo. Sabse common formatting error hai empty assistant message — whitespace strip karne ke baad assistant ka content khaali reh jaata hai. Ye tab hota hai jab teacher model ka blank response filtering se slip ho gaya ho. Aise examples ko training se pehle fix karo, warna training me errors aur kharab seekh milegi.

TRL ka SFTTrainer

TRL (Transformer Reinforcement Learning library) instruction fine-tuning ke liye dominant open-source framework ban gaya hai. Uska SFTTrainer do formats accept karta hai: conversational format (messages field wali rows) aur preformatted text strings. Conversational format behtar hai, kyunki trainer tumhare diye hue tokenizer se khud apply_chat_template call karke template apply kar deta hai. Book ka worked example Gemma 4 E4B-it par hai:

  • Model: bf16 me load (FP32 me 8B params lagbhag 32 GB lete), device_map="auto" se layers GPU memory me distribute hote hain.
  • Epochs: 3 — fine-tuning me 3 se zyada ka matlab aam taur par memorization hota hai, learning nahi.
  • Batch: per-device batch size 4, gradient accumulation 4 steps — effective batch 16, batch 4 ki memory cost par.
  • Learning rate: 2e-5 — ye full fine-tune ke liye hai; LoRA aam taur par isse lagbhag 10x zyada use karta hai.
  • Warmup: 5% — pehle steps me learning rate dheere badhta hai, taaki early noisy gradients model ko galat direction me na le jaayein.
  • Evaluation aur saving: har 100 steps par validation, har 200 steps par checkpoint — crash hone par 200 steps se zyada progress kabhi nahi khoyega.
  • Max length: 2,048 tokens — isse lambi examples truncate ho jaati hain.

Alpaca ko SFTTrainer ke saath

Agar data Alpaca format me hai, to dataset.map(alpaca_to_messages, remove_columns=...) se ek baar convert karo — dataset me messages field aa jaata hai aur SFTTrainer use native chat template ke saath handle kar leta hai. Dhyaan do: ye code train/validation split khud nahi karta, woh tumhe apni requirement ke hisaab se karna hai.

Yaad rakho: TRL abstraction bahut kuch chhupa deta hai, jo convenient hai lekin errors trace karna mushkil kar deta hai. Training se pehle dataset ko validation tools se check karo — nahi to training ke beech me errors ki baarish hogi.
SOURCESource: Fine-Tuning AI, O'Reilly, Chapter 6 — Preparing Your Dataset for Fine-Tuning
← Previous06.1 · Completion vs Chat, and Chat Templates→ Next06.3 · Loss Masking, Frameworks, and Validation
06.3Chapter 6 · Preparing Your Dataset for Fine-Tuning

Loss Masking, Frameworks, and Validation

Data format ho gaya, trainer bhi mil gaya — ab ek subtle lekin bahut powerful concept: loss masking. Iske bina model tumhare sawaal repeat karna seekhne me apna training budget kharch kar dega.

Loss masking kyun zaroori hai

Poori conversation par train karte waqt loss har token par compute hota hai — instruction, system prompt aur role markers par bhi. Matlab model ko optimize kiya ja raha hai user ke sawaal reproduce karne ke liye, jo bilkul ulta hai tum jo chahte ho. Tum chahte ho model achhe jawab de, isse koi farak nahi padta ki woh sawaal ki exact phrasing reproduce kar sakta hai ya nahi. Loss masking me instruction tokens ke labels ko -100 set kar diya jaata hai — PyTorch ka convention jiska matlab hai "loss calculation me is token ko ignore karo". Model instruction ko context ke roop me padh to sakta hai, lekin gradient update sirf answer tokens ko kitni achhi tarah predict kiya, usse aata hai. Ye effect khaas taur par tab strong hota hai jab instructions lambi aur answers chhote hon — medical Q&A me aisa aam hai, jahan detailed patient question answer se bahut lamba ho sakta hai.

Collator aur prefix-tokenization trap

Implement karne ke liye aam taur par ek data collator use hota hai — woh component jo individual tokenized examples ko batches me assemble karta hai, padding handle karta hai. DataCollatorForCompletionOnlyLM response template ke basis par masking karta hai. Ek validate_masking helper se tum DataLoader se ek batch lekar har token ke saath TRAIN ya MASK status print kar sakte ho — sirf assistant ke response tokens par TRAIN hona chahiye. Agar system prompt ya instruction tokens par TRAIN dikhe, to masking kaam nahi kar rahi: response template ka format debug karo ya messaging format badlo. Ek sneaky trap hai prefix tokenization: standalone encode karne par template ka pehla token alag tokenize hota hai, kyunki tokenizer ne usse pehle wale newline ke saath merge kar liya hota hai. Fix hai template ko context me encode karna (preceding newline ke saath) aur phir pehla token slice karke hata dena, aur resulting IDs ko string ke bajaye collator ko dena.

Axolotl — YAML-driven training

Axolotl ek YAML-configured framework hai jo bahut se data formats, base models aur PEFT methods support karta hai. Code likhne ke bajaye tum config file banate ho — reproducible, version-controlled training setups ke liye ideal. Book ka example Gemma 4 E4B-it, messages-format JSONL, sequence_len: 1024, QLoRA (rank 16, alpha 32), micro batch 2, gradient accumulation 4, learning rate 2e-4, cosine schedule ke saath hai. Sabse important line hai train_on_inputs: false — ye Axolotl ka loss masking ka equivalent hai, jo instruction tuning ke liye hamesha false hona chahiye. Ek limitation: Axolotl NVIDIA aur CUDA se heavily tied hai — uska config loader startup par CUDA-specific functions call karta hai, to ye Mac ya CPU-only machines par nahi chalega. Mac par tum config prepare aur validate kar sakte ho, lekin training CUDA machine ya cloud par karni hogi.

Unsloth — speed aur kam memory

Unsloth speed aur memory efficiency par focused library hai — custom CUDA kernels aur aggressive memory optimization se. Uska FastLanguageModel API Hugging Face model-loading step ka drop-in replacement hai, baaki SFTTrainer interface wahi rehta hai. 4-bit me load karne se 8B model lagbhag 5 GB VRAM me aa jaata hai, to free Colab T4 (16 GB) par bhi achhe se chalta hai. Loss masking ke liye train_on_responses_only hai, jo Gemma 4 ke <|turn>user aur <|turn>model markers use karta hai. Yahan version drift ka warning hai: purani Gemma generations ke turn markers alag the. Agar tum purane strings use karoge, to kuch crash nahi hoga — markers kabhi mile hi nahi, koi masking nahi hogi, aur model apna budget patient ke sawaal reproduce karna seekhne me kharch karega. Isliye jab bhi model badlo — yahan tak ki same family ka version bhi — ek example par apply_chat_template ka output print karke turn markers ko real formatted text se padho. Kabhi memory se type mat karo. Unsloth ke SFTTrainer ko explicit formatting_func chahiye hota hai, kyunki woh messages format ko vanilla TRL ki tarah auto-detect nahi karta.

Splits sahi tareeke se, aur validation

Split ke liye seed 42 use karo taaki har baar wahi random set bane. Synthetic data ke liye category ke hisaab se split karo — random split se near-duplicate test examples training me leak ho sakte hain. Validation me book ki check: 580 / 580 examples valid, token lengths p50 435, p90 510, p99 560, max 700 — matlab max length 2,048 ke saath data comfortably fit hota hai. Structural failures (missing keys, empty messages lists) ka matlab hai conversion code me problem hai. Aur sabse important principle: pipeline ko fix karo, records ko nahi — validation fail ho to conversion code theek karo, individual examples ko haath se edit mat karo. Training se pehle tokenized examples ko seedhe inspect karo.

Yaad rakho: agar masking kaam nahi kar rahi, to model sawaal yaad kar raha hai, jawab nahi seekh raha. TRAIN / MASK inspection training se pehle karo — baad me pata chalna bahut mehenga padta hai.
SOURCESource: Fine-Tuning AI, O'Reilly, Chapter 6 — Preparing Your Dataset for Fine-Tuning
← Previous06.2 · Converting Data and Training with TRL→ Next07 · The Mechanics of Adaptation
07Chapter 7 · The Mechanics of Adaptation

The Mechanics of Adaptation

Data taiyaar hai, format sahi hai — ab sawaal hai: model ko kaise adapt karein? Full fine-tuning, jisme har weight update hota hai, kagaz par sabse powerful lagta hai. Lekin uski keemat itni zyada hai ki zyadaatar logon ke liye woh out of reach hai. Is chapter ka jawab hai parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) — aur usme sabse upar LoRA.

Full fine-tuning ki teen problems

  • Memory problem: 8B model ke full fine-tune ke liye 68–72 GB VRAM chahiye. Adam optimizer states akele 16-bit me 48 GB lete hain (FP32 me 64 GB), gradients 16 GB, activations 4–8 GB. Training me inference se bahut zyada memory lagti hai, kyunki optimizer states, gradients aur activations sab ek saath pile ho jaate hain.
  • Catastrophic forgetting: saare weights update karne se model nayi task seekhte-seekhte apni general abilities kho sakta hai — purana knowledge overwrite ho jaata hai.
  • Storage problem: har full fine-tune model ki ek poori copy hoti hai — 40 GB se zyada. Har expert ke liye ek alag 40 GB copy rakhna scale nahi karta.

PEFT landscape

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning ka idea simple hai: base model ke zyadaatar weights ko frozen rakho aur sirf ek chhota sa trainable hissa update karo. Teen methods aam hain — prefix tuning, adapters aur LoRA. Prefix tuning aur adapters pehle aaye, lekin practice me dono ko LoRA ne largely replace kar diya hai. LoRA aaj LLM fine-tuning ka dominant PEFT method hai, aur is chapter ka focus bhi wahi hai.

LoRA ka core idea

LoRA base weights ko chhoota hi nahi — woh unke saath ek chhota sa trainable branch jod deta hai. Training ke dauraan sirf woh branch seekhta hai, base model frozen rehta hai. Result ek chhota, portable adapter hota hai jo base model par lagaya ya hataya ja sakta hai. Ek hi base model par alag-alag tasks ke liye alag-alag adapters rakh sakte ho, aur inference time par unhe swap kar sakte ho — bina poora model dobara load kiye. Agle do sections me LoRA ki maths, uske hyperparameters, QLoRA aur DoRA ko detail me dekhenge.

Yaad rakho: full fine-tuning har weight ko badalta hai — mehenga, bhoolne wala aur store karne me bhaari. PEFT ka idea hai base ko frozen rakho, sirf ek chhota specialist hissa train karo.

07.1Chapter 7 · The Mechanics of Adaptation

LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation

LoRA — Low-Rank Adaptation — ka idea deceptively simple hai: poori weight matrix ko update karne ke bajaye, sirf uska ek low-rank update seekho. Result comparable hota hai full fine-tune ke, lekin trainable parameters ka ek chhota sa fraction use karke.

Maths: ΔW = BA

Ek layer ki weight matrix W ko update karne ke bajaye, LoRA update ko do chhoti matrices me factor kar deta hai: ΔW = BA, jahan B ek d × r matrix hai aur A ek r × d matrix, aur r hai rank. Example: 2,560-dimension wali layer me rank 16 ke saath ye sirf 81,920 parameters hote hain, poori 6.5 million wali matrix ke bajaye — lagbhag 80× reduction. Sabse bada demonstration: 175B-parameter wale model ko sirf uske weights ke 0.01% trainable rakh kar adapt kiya gaya, full fine-tune ke comparable results ke saath. Forward pass aisa hota hai: h = W₀x + (α/r)·BAx — original frozen weights ka output, plus LoRA branch ka scaled output. A ko Kaiming uniform se initialise kiya jaata hai aur B zeros se shuru hota hai, to training ki shuruaat me adapter kuch bhi change nahi karta — model bilkul base model jaisa behave karta hai, aur dheere-dheere seekhta hai.

Kahan apply karein — target modules

Original approach attention projections par focus karta tha, lekin book ka default hai all-linear: attention ke q / k / v / o projections plus feed-forward ke gate / up / down — model ki saari linear layers. Embeddings aur language-model head (final output projection) ko aam taur par targets se bahar rakha jaata hai.

Merging — zero inference overhead

LoRA ki sabse attractive property hai merging: W_merged = W₀ + (α/r)·BA se adapter ko base weights me fold kar diya jaata hai. Merge karne ke baad model ki structure bilkul wahi rehti hai — koi extra layer nahi, koi additional latency nahi. Tumhara pehle likha inference code minor modifications ke saath kaam karta hai. Ya tum merge na karke adapter ko alag bhi rakh sakte ho aur inference time par dynamically swap kar sakte ho — ek hi base model se multiple task-specific variants serve karne ka powerful technique, jise book baad me detail me cover karta hai.

Ye kaam kyun karta hai — corporation analogy

Mathematical explanation hai ki weight updates ki intrinsic dimensionality low hoti hai. Lekin intuition ke liye book ek analogy deta hai: pretrained model ko ek badi corporation samjho, hazaaron employees ke saath, har ek ka well-defined job. Full fine-tuning matlab har employee ko naye role ke liye retrain karna — mehenga, slow, aur risky, kyunki kuch critical knowledge kho sakta hai. LoRA matlab specialists ki ek chhoti team hire karna jo existing crew ke saath kaam kare. Specialists kisi ko replace nahi karte; woh task-specific expertise add karte hain. Original log apna kaam karte rehte hain, specialists nayi requirements sambhalte hain. Rank (r) control karta hai kitne specialists hire karne hain — task cover karne ke liye kaafi, lekin total headcount se bahut kam. Aur zaroorat padne par specialists ko augment kiya ya swap kiya ja sakta hai.

Yaad rakho: LoRA poori matrix ko update nahi karta — woh ΔW = BA seekhta hai, jahan rank r adapter ki capacity hai. Chhota adapter, frozen base, aur merge karne par zero extra latency.
SOURCESource: Fine-Tuning AI, O'Reilly, Chapter 7 — The Mechanics of Adaptation
← Previous07 · The Mechanics of Adaptation→ Next07.2 · Rank, Alpha, Dropout, QLoRA, and DoRA
07.2Chapter 7 · The Mechanics of Adaptation

Rank, Alpha, Dropout, QLoRA, and DoRA

LoRA samajhna aasan hai, lekin use sahi tareeke se configure karna hi farak banata hai — ek achha fine-tune aur ek kharab fine-tune ke beech ka farak aksar inhi hyperparameters me hota hai.

Rank (r) — adapter ki capacity

Rank sabse important LoRA hyperparameter hai: ye control karta hai adapter kitni information encode kar sakta hai. Zyada rank matlab zyada trainable parameters, lekin zyada memory aur compute ki keemat par. Common values 4 se 256 tak hoti hain. Gemma 4 E4B ke liye book ki guidance:

  • Rank 8: simple tasks ke liye reasonable starting point — tone adjust karna, style transfer, ya chhote dataset par fine-tune jahan model ko domain ka base knowledge pehle se strong hai.
  • Rank 16–32: zyadaatar tasks ka sweet spot. Medical Q&A project ke liye book rank 16 se shuru karta hai — specific answering style aur kuch domain patterns seekhne ke liye kaafi.
  • Rank 64–128: complex tasks jahan model ko substantially naya knowledge seekhna hai — jaise nayi programming language ya highly specialized domain jiska unique vocabulary model ne pehle zyada dekha hi nahi.
  • Rank 256+: full fine-tuning ki capacity ke kareeb pahunch jaata hai aur rarely zaroori hota hai. Agar itna rank chahiye, to shayad full fine-tune behtar hai.

Rank aur performance ka relation linear nahi hai — woh plateau karta hai. Ek point ke baad additional rank se diminishing returns milte hain. Woh point dhoondhna experiment karne layak hai.

Alpha, dropout, bias aur task type

  • Alpha (α): scaling factor α/r control karta hai ki LoRA update output ko kitna influence kare. Convention hai alpha = 2r — rank 16 ho to alpha 32, scaling factor 2. Training me alpha ke bajaye learning rate adjust karo.
  • Target modules: Gemma ke liye all-linear standard starting point hai. Embeddings aur LM head ko targets se bahar rakho — unhe modify karne se instabilities aa sakti hain.
  • Dropout: adapter ke output par standard dropout. 1,000 se kam examples ho (jaise hamara medical Q&A) to 0.05–0.1 reasonable hai; bade datasets par 0 bhi chal sakta hai.
  • Bias: "none" matlab koi bias parameter train nahi hota — sabse memory-efficient setting aur LoRA ka standard. "all" ya "lora_only" options bhi hain.
  • Task type: Gemma decoder-only model hai, to CAUSAL_LM — model next token predict karta hai, pichhle tokens ke basis par.

Worked config — kitna chhota hai adapter?

Rank 16, alpha 32, all-linear targets, dropout 0.05, bias none, CAUSAL_LM wali config Gemma 4 E4B par 38,879,232 trainable parameters deti hai, total 7,979,980,064 me se — sirf 0.4872%, lagbhag 150 MB ka adapter. get_peft_model base weights ko freeze kar deta hai (requires_grad=False) aur sirf LoRA matrices trainable rehti hain.

QLoRA — base ko 4-bit me load karo

LoRA trainable parameters ko chhota karta hai, lekin base model phir bhi load karna padta hai: Gemma 4 E4B bf16 me lagbhag 16 GB VRAM leta hai, aur optimizer plus activations mila kar LoRA setup 20–24 GB tak pahunch jaata hai — 24 GB wale GPU ke edge par. QLoRA base model ko NF4 4-bit precision me load karke is problem ko solve karta hai. Uske teen ingredients hain: NormalFloat4 (NF4) — neural network weights ki normal distribution ke liye design kiya gaya 4-bit data type; double quantization — quantization constants ko bhi quantize karna, jo lagbhag 1.5% bachata hai (65B model par lagbhag 3 GB); aur paged optimizers — optimizer GPU aur CPU memory share karta hai, taaki memory spikes se out-of-memory errors na aayein. Gemma 4 E4B par QLoRA VRAM requirement ko 10–12 GB tak le aata hai. Ye clean 4× reduction nahi hai, kyunki Gemma 4 ke bahut se parameters embedding tables me hain jo quantize nahi hote. Setup me BitsAndBytesConfig (load_in_4bit, nf4, compute dtype bf16, double quant) aur prepare_model_for_kbit_training use hota hai — ye quantized base par gradient checkpointing aur stability ke liye essential hai.

DoRA — magnitude aur direction alag-alag

DoRA (Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation) har weight ko magnitude aur direction components me split karke unhe separately adapt karta hai. Isse LoRA par 1–4% improvement milta hai, bina kisi inference cost ke — enable karna sirf use_dora=True hai. Comparison me: LoRA 16-bit, lagbhag 50M params, 20–24 GB; QLoRA 4-bit NF4, lagbhag 50M params, 10–12 GB; QLoRA + DoRA 4-bit, lagbhag 36M+ params, 10–12 GB. Book ki guidance: QLoRA se shuru karo agar VRAM kam hai; VRAM budget ho to seedha LoRA, aur phir DoRA ko optimization step ke roop me add karo. Aam pitfalls: galat target modules, embeddings ko include karna, ya quantized model ko prepare kiye bina train karna.

Yaad rakho: rank 16–32 sweet spot hai, alpha = 2r rakho, aur chhote GPU par QLoRA se shuru karo. Bada rank automatically behtar nahi hota — performance plateau karta hai.
